items.title: Q1 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Nirad C. Chaudhuri
items.stem:
Identify from the following the work Nirad C. Chaudhuri called "the finest novel in the
English language with an Indian theme"

structured.lead:
Identify from the following the work Nirad C. Chaudhuri called "the finest novel in the
English language with an Indian theme"
structured.options_hint: Kim Passage to India Train to Pakistan P

options: Private Life of an Indian Prince
items.explanation: In a 1957 essay for Encounter, Indian writer Nirad C. Chaudhuri praised Rudyard Kipling's Kim (1901) as 'the finest novel in the English language with an Indian theme'. He admired Kipling's vivid and authentic portrayal of North Indian landscapes, common people, and spiritual life.

items.title: Q2 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit II: Poetry · Robert Browning
items.stem:
Who is the author of the poem "The Defence of Lucknow" dealing with the siege of
Lucknow, one of the terrible incidents of the Indian Mutiny ?

structured.lead:
Who is the author of the poem "The Defence of Lucknow" dealing with the siege of
Lucknow, one of the terrible incidents of the Indian Mutiny ?
structured.options_hint: Rudyard Kipling Edward Lear Alfred Lord

items.explanation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote the patriotic ballad 'The Defence of Lucknow' in 1879. The poem commemorates the British garrison's eighty-seven-day resistance at the Residency during the 1857 Siege of Lucknow.

items.title: Q3 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following theorists holds that metaphor and metonymy are the two
fundamental structures of language ?

structured.lead: Who among the following theorists holds that metaphor and metonymy are the two fundamental structures of language ?
structured.options_hint: Ferdinand de Saussure Austin Roman Jakob

items.explanation: In his landmark 1956 essay 'Two Aspects of Language and Two Types of Aphasic Disturbances', Russian-American linguist Roman Jakobson argued that language operates along two fundamental axes: metaphor (based on similarity and selection) and metonymy (based on contiguity and combination).

items.title: Q5 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Ruth Prawer Jhabvala

structured.lead: Which among the following texts can be characterised as a lesbian Bildungsroman ?
structured.options_hint: Angela Carter, The Magic Toyshop Sylvia

options: Jeanette Winterson, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit
Ruth Pawar Jhabvala, Heat and Dust
items.explanation: Jeanette Winterson's semi-autobiographical debut novel Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit (1985) is a classic lesbian Bildungsroman. It follows Jeanette, an adopted girl raised in a strict English Pentecostal community, as she discovers her lesbian identity and comes of age.

items.title: Q6 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · John Locke, Francis Bacon, John Milton

structured.options_hint: Paradise Lost - The Advancement of Learn

options: Paradise Lost - The Advancement of Learning - An Essay Concerning Human Understanding - MacFlecknoe

items.explanation: The correct chronological order of publication is Francis Bacon's The Advancement of Learning (1605), John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), John Dryden's satire Mac Flecknoe (1682), and John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689/1690).

items.explanation: In Edgar Allan Poe's narrative poem 'The Raven' (1845), the distraught unnamed speaker sits reading at midnight while mourning the death of his beloved, 'the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore'.

items.title: Q8 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Macbeth who was "untimely ripped" from his mother's womb ?

structured.lead: In Shakespeare's Macbeth who was "untimely ripped" from his mother's womb ?
structured.options_hint: Macbeth Macduff Duncan Malcolm

items.explanation: In Act V, Scene 8 of William Shakespeare's Macbeth (c. 1606), Macduff reveals that he was 'from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd' (born by Caesarean section). This fulfills the witches' prophecy that no man 'of woman born' could harm Macbeth.

items.title: Q9 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit II: Poetry · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Alexander Pope revised The Rape of the Lock three times. In the final revision of the
poem in 1717 he inserted a speech by

structured.lead: Alexander Pope revised The Rape of the Lock three times. In the final revision of the poem in 1717 he inserted a speech by
structured.options_hint: Belinda Clarissa Betty Thalestris

items.explanation: In the 1717 edition of The Rape of the Lock, Alexander Pope added Clarissa's grave moral speech in Canto V ('to open more clearly the MORAL of the Poem'). In it, Clarissa urges Belinda to value good humor and virtue over fleeting physical beauty.

items.explanation: The 'Prelude' to George Eliot's novel Middlemarch (1871–72) invokes the history of Saint Theresa of Ávila, using her passionate spiritual ambition to introduce the plight of modern 'later-born Theresas' like Dorothea Brooke whose noble aspirations are constrained by society.

punished, was devised by

structured.lead: The term, "poetic justice," to designate the idea that the good are rewarded and the evil punished, was devised by
structured.options_hint: Aristotle John Dryden Thomas Rhymer Ben

items.explanation: The English neoclassical critic Thomas Rymer coined the term 'poetic justice' in his essay The Tragedies of the Last Age Consider'd (1678) to argue that literature should distribute moral rewards to the virtuous and punishments to the wicked.

items.explanation: Miles Coverdale produced the first complete printed English translation of the Bible in 1535, building upon William Tyndale's earlier translations of the New Testament and parts of the Old Testament.

items.explanation: Virginia Woolf's modernist novel To the Lighthouse (1927) is divided into three sections: 'The Window', 'Time Passes', and 'The Lighthouse'. 'The Sky' is not a part of the novel.

items.title: Q23 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Patrick White
items.stem:
Which novel by Patrick White is based on the story of Ludwig Leichhardt, the Prussian
naturalist who explored Australia in the mid-1840s, in which White's fictional hero says
when asked about navigation - "The Map? I will first make it" ?

structured.lead: Which novel by Patrick White is based on the story of Ludwig Leichhardt, the Prussian naturalist who explored Australia in the mid-1840s, in which White's fictional hero says when asked about navigation - "The Map? I will first make it" ?
structured.options_hint: The Tree of Man Voss Riders in the Chari

items.explanation: Patrick White's historical novel Voss (1957) is modelled on the nineteenth-century Prussian explorer Ludwig Leichhardt, who vanished while crossing the Australian outback. Its visionary protagonist Johann Ulrich Voss famously declares, 'The map? I will first make it.'

items.title: Q24 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Golding

structured.lead: Who among the following is not a character in William Golding's Lord of the Flies ?
structured.options_hint: Ralph Piggy Peter Jack

items.explanation: Ralph, Piggy, and Jack are central characters in William Golding's Lord of the Flies (1954). Peter is not a character in Golding's novel; rather, Peter, Ralph, and Jack were the three boys in R. M. Ballantyne's adventure novel The Coral Island (1857), which Golding's book subverts.

items.title: Q30 · Jan 2017 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: What is a trochee ?

structured.lead: What is a trochee ?
structured.options_hint: A two syllable foot of verse with two he

options: A two syllable foot of verse with two heavy stresses
A two syllable foot of verse in which the stress falls on the first syllable
A six line stanza in which the rhyme sounds are all identical
items.explanation: In English prosody, a trochee (trochaic foot) is a two-syllable metrical foot consisting of a stressed (accented) first syllable followed by an unstressed syllable (DUM-da), as in 'Tíger, tíger, búrning bríght.'
